subject: physics
title: Diffraction and diffraction gratings
key_idea: Waves spread out through gaps and round obstacles, most when the gap is about one wavelength. A diffraction grating with slit spacing d gives sharp maxima at angles where d sin θ = nλ.

blocks.text: Waves spread out when they pass through a gap or round the edge of an obstacle. This is diffraction, and all waves do it.

items.meaning: The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or round an obstacle.
Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. The new wavefront is the line that touches the wavelets.

items: The effect is greatest when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength.
A gap much wider than λ gives little spreading: the wave goes through almost straight, with a shadow at the sides.
A narrower gap, or a longer wavelength, gives more spreading.
The wavelength and frequency do not change. Only the direction does.

items.text: A plane wavefront reaches a gap.
Each point in the gap sends out secondary wavelets in all forward directions.
The wavelets overlap. Near the edges there is no wavelet to join the line, so the new wavefront curves and spreads into the shadow.
Behind an obstacle, wavelets from points beside its edge spread into the shadow region, so the wave bends round it.

blocks.text: Ripple tanks show this: water waves of fixed wavelength pass through a gap whose width is varied.

items: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is comparable to λ.
Huygens' construction treats each point on a wavefront as a source of wavelets.

blocks.text: Light through a single narrow slit forms a pattern on a screen. It has a wide, bright central maximum with fainter maxima either side.

items: The central maximum is wider and much brighter than the others.
A narrower slit gives a wider central maximum.
A longer wavelength gives a wider central maximum.
With white light the central maximum is white, and the fringes at the sides are coloured, with red furthest out.
Narrower slit or longer wavelength means a wider central maximum.
White light gives a white centre with coloured edges.

blocks.text: A diffraction grating has many equally spaced slits. It gives sharp, bright maxima at precise angles.

items.text: Neighbouring slits are a distance d apart, where d = 1 / (lines per metre).
At angle θ, light from adjacent slits differs in path by d sin θ.
The waves from all slits add in phase when this path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ.

blocks.label: Grating equation
where: θ = angle from the straight-through direction to the nth maximum

items: The n = 0 maximum is straight on. Orders n = 1, 2, ... lie symmetrically on both sides.
The highest order seen is the largest whole number n with nλ < d, because sin θ cannot exceed 1.
A grating with more lines per millimetre has a smaller d, so the maxima are further apart.
Longer wavelengths are diffracted through larger angles, so white light is split into a spectrum of each order.

diagram.alt: Find sin of the angle to a grating maximum.
diagram.question: A grating has {N} lines per mm. Light of wavelength {lam} nm falls normally on it. Calculate sin θ for the order n = {n} maximum.

items: Gratings give sharper and brighter maxima than a double slit, so wavelengths can be measured more precisely.
Gratings split light into spectra for finding which elements are in a star or a lamp, and for measuring wavelengths.
d sin θ = nλ, with d = 1 / lines per metre.
A grating gives sharp maxima that are good for measuring wavelength.

checks.q: State what happens to the central maximum of a single-slit diffraction pattern when the slit is made narrower.
checks.a: The central maximum becomes wider (and less bright).

checks.q: A grating has 300 lines per mm. Light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum.
Explain why a diffraction grating is better than a double slit for measuring a wavelength.
checks.a: The maxima are much sharper and brighter, so their angles can be measured more precisely.

items: Derive d sin θ = nλ: the path difference between light from adjacent slits is d sin θ, and a maximum needs this to be nλ.
A plane transmission grating is used at normal incidence. The use of a spectrometer is not needed.
The graph of intensity against angle for a single slit is not required.
Know experiments that show diffraction, such as water waves in a ripple tank through a gap.
State the effect of gap width relative to wavelength: a gap much larger than λ gives almost no spreading; a gap about λ spreads waves widely.
Use a transmission grating to determine the wavelength of light: shine a laser normally on it, measure the distance from the grating to the screen and the distance from the centre to a maximum.
Find θ from tan θ = (distance along the screen) ÷ (distance to the screen), then use d sin θ = nλ.
Proof of the grating equation is not required. A spectrometer is not needed.
